description:
I'm a student interested in engineering and AI/ML. I enjoy building projects that combine programming, data science, and real-world applications.

For NASA Space Apps, I'm developing a web application focused on harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations. So far, I've built an interactive dashboard using React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, and trained a Random Forest regression model to explore relationships between satellite observations.
summary:
Fire Observations is an interactive web platform designed to make long-term wildfire activity easier to explore and understand using NASA FIRMS active-fire observations from MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments.
The platform organizes satellite hotspot detections into an accessible dashboard where users can explore historical activity, examine seasonal and yearly trends, compare sensor observations, and investigate different statistical harmonization approaches. It also incorporates a machine-learning baseline to explore relationships between satellite observations and predict brightness values.
By bringing multiple satellite datasets and analytical tools into one interface, the platform addresses the challenge of making fire activity patterns more understandable across sensors and over time. Understanding these patterns can support environmental monitoring, research, and informed decision-making. The project demonstrates how accessible data visualization, statistical analysis, and machine learning can help transform large volumes of satellite observations into meaningful insights.
details:
My project is an interactive platform for exploring historical fire activity in the United States using NASA FIRMS active-fire observations from MODIS and VIIRS satellites. It brings together satellite datasets spanning multiple years and provides visualizations that help users understand patterns in fire detections, compare satellite observations, and investigate changes over time.

The platform includes an overview dashboard, interactive detection map, tools for comparing sensor data, a historical activity calendar heatmap, and model results. Users can explore monthly and annual patterns, analyze differences between satellite instruments, and identify periods of unusually high activity. Our historical analysis covers 2000–2025 and shows significant variation between years, including a drastic spike in September 2020. I also trained a Random Forest regression model on more than 713,000 observations from 2026 to explore relationships between detection characteristics and brightness. The model achieved an R² of 0.906 and an MAE of approximately 4.54 K on a test set.

The project's main benefit is making large satellite datasets easier to explore and interpret without requiring users to process raw files/datasets. Researchers, students, and other interested users can use the platform to investigate historical patterns, identify unusual periods, and explore differences between satellite sensors. These findings can provide context for further environmental research, although detection counts should not be interpreted as confirmed numbers of individual fires.

I developed the platform using React, JavaScript, and Tailwind CSS, with Python and pandas for data processing and scikit-learn for machine learning. NASA FIRMS provided the satellite observations, while the dashboard uses interactive charts, maps, and historical visualizations to present the results after testing scikit-learn's Random Forest Regressor model.

The creative aspect of the project is that it brings data exploration, satellite comparison, and machine learning analysis together in one accessible website. Rather than presenting satellite detections as various datasets, the platform allows users to examine them across time and sensor types. During development, I considered differences between satellite instruments, data quality, confidence classifications, geographic coverage, and the limitations of comparing detection counts across sensors. I also aimed to make the visualizations understandable while being transparent about the limitations of the underlying data and analysis.

Ultimately, my goal is to make satellite-based fire observations more accessible and provide a foundation for improved cross-sensor analysis and long-term environmental monitoring.
